about.intro: I grew up in Marsh End, studied business information systems at Marsh End College and joined Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls in 2019 to answer the order-desk phone beside Tilly Brandt. I kept a log of every order we had to key twice, and in 2021 I took that habit to Quillfold Supply Co. as a product analyst. In 2023 Gordie Pruitt, our regional manager, asked me back to run customer ordering as a product manager, armed with a whiteboard acronym I politely retired. In 2025 I started a weekend diploma at Thistlewood Institute of Management to strengthen the strategy side.
about.now: Writing Margin Notes on Fridays, practising violin before breakfast and training for the February half marathon.

suggested-routing-rules.context: Pinewick sells paper, toner and stationery to about 1,900 office customers across the Mid-Valley. Most reorder the same handful of items every month, and most of them phone the order desk, where the orders are keyed in by hand.
suggested-routing-rules.problem: Of 38,000 orders in 2023, 61% repeated at least four-fifths of the previous order, yet 72% of those still came in by phone. A phone reorder took a median of 6 minutes to key, and about 1 in 12 carried a typo, such as 40 cartons of A3 instead of 4.
what_i_did: Pulled two years of order history and grouped accounts by how closely each order repeated the last.
Interviewed 14 office managers. Most knew their usual order by heart but could never find the login.
Wrote the PRD for the Reorder Button: it shows the usual order with last month's quantities and lets the customer confirm with one tap.
Shaped the confirmation card with design and agreed a nightly rebuild of each account's usual order with engineering to keep cost down. Gordie wanted to name the feature SYNERGY; we did not.

decisions.choice: One-tap confirmation instead of automatic reordering
decisions.why: Office managers would not let a system spend their budget unattended. A tap they make is an order they can explain to their own finance team.
Brought the estimate down from two quarters to a single quarter, and a customer's usual order only shifts month to month anyway.

results.note: 300 pilot accounts vs matched control, 8 weeks
of 3,400 repeat orders in the pilot

suggested-routing-rules.learned: The quantity line mattered more than the button. Take-up climbed from 31% to 54% after the card began flagging any quantity that jumped more than 20%, as in "40 cartons, usually 4?".
suggested-routing-rules.next: Extend the button to standing orders for toner, where customers make the same slips on a calendar.
suggested-routing-rules.my_role: Product Manager, discovery lead and PRD author

slotwise.context: Pinewick's single warehouse door served delivery vans and customer pickups with no schedule. Monday mornings were the worst, and the dock crew had to improvise.
slotwise.problem: On a typical Monday about 70 vehicles arrived between 8 and 11 am for a dock that could load 12 an hour. Drivers waited a median of 48 minutes, and the ones who gave up came back at peak the next day.
what_i_did: Stood on the dock for four mornings with Wendell's crew and logged every arrival and loading time.
Built the booking flow on a messaging thread, with a spreadsheet as the schedule and a small script sending reminders.
Sent a reminder the night before that let drivers move to another slot with one tap.
Kept it running for ten weeks, with a Friday check-in on the dock to sort out whatever had gone wrong.

decisions.choice: A message thread, not an app
decisions.why: Every driver already had the messaging app, and nobody wanted to install anything to collect a pallet of copy paper.
Wendell could read and edit the schedule on the dock without any training.

slotwise.learned: The reminder outperformed the booking itself: late arrivals dropped once a driver could move a slot with one tap instead of phoning Tilly.
slotwise.next: Marla's biggest customers want same-day pickups. I would test a paid express slot before building anything else.

uc-reschedules.context: Pinewick Print Studio makes letterheads, invoices and event programmes for local businesses. Reprints ran at 7.4%, most of them found after delivery. Each one costs paper, press time and a very polite apology.
uc-reschedules.problem: Customers did not know what they were approving. The proof was a PDF emailed late in the afternoon, and many ticked approved to keep their date. Gordie's own business cards once went out reading "Regional Manger".
what_i_did: Read 40 reprint tickets and coded every cause.
Called 31 customers who had needed a reprint in the last quarter.
Spent nine days on the press floor, two of them full shifts, to watch the proof step from the operators' side.
Designed a proof page that highlights the three fields customers get wrong (name, phone, date) and asks for a tick on each.
Set up the pilot with the press supervisor on two presses with matched control presses, and a daily funnel in Mixpanel for proofs sent, ticked and reprinted.

decisions.choice: Highlight three fields, not the whole proof
decisions.why: Tickets showed that nearly all errors sat in names, phone numbers and dates. A full-page checklist would have been ignored.

decisions.choice: Send proofs at 10 am, not 4 pm
decisions.why: Late-day proofs were approved in a hurry to keep the date, so we moved them to when people still had time to read.
Job mix changes reprint rates a lot, so a simple before-and-after would have misled us.

uc-reschedules.learned: Highlighting the name did more than anything else. Customers said they skipped it because it was obviously right, which was the whole problem.
uc-reschedules.next: Roll the proof page out to the other four presses, and test a read-aloud phone proof for rush jobs.

case-sprint.context: A 48-hour product case at Thistlewood Institute of Management in spring 2025, against 31 teams. New small-office customers were leaving an online stationery catalogue before a first order, and the brief asked for a diagnosis and a fix.
what_i_did: Led a team of four through the 48 hours.
Held 22 short conversations with office managers at the Larchmont Falls trade fair over two days, each walking through their last abandoned basket.
Placed each conversation on a map of the basket steps, then estimated the size of the leak from published figures.
Proposed a first-order flow and pitched it to the judges.
case-sprint.problem: Every conversation circled back to the final page. One office manager put it this way: "Nobody told me about carriage until I had built the whole basket." New customers filled a cart, met a charge they had not budgeted for and left.

decisions.choice: Show carriage in the basket total on the very first page for new accounts
decisions.why: The complaint was about when the charge appeared, so we moved the charge forward instead of proposing a discount.

case-sprint.learned: Two days of quick chats in one hall beat the published figures and led us to one page.

assignment-health.context: Three Quillfold sales teams reviewed quote turnaround every Monday, but each timed it from a different moment, so the huddle turned into an argument about whether quotes were getting faster or slower.
what_i_did: Agreed four shared metrics with the three team leads over two lunches.
Built the queries in Postgres and put them on a single weekly Metabase dashboard.
Retired the five spreadsheets the teams had each been keeping.

results.note: use it in every Monday huddle

decisions.why: Each team owned a different stage of a quote, and one blended score would hide whose number moved.

decisions.choice: Agree the definitions before building anything
decisions.why: The teams already had numbers. What they lacked was a shared start and stop point for the clock.

assignment-health.learned: Most of the effort went into agreeing when the clock starts. Once that was signed off, the dashboard took days.

hrtech-pricing.context: Harbourton Label Works sold labels at one flat price per roll and wanted to move to subscription tiers. This was a six-week live project from Thistlewood Institute with two classmates.
what_i_did: Interviewed 14 office managers about how they buy labels and what they would pay for.
Fielded a Van Westendorp price survey and got 120 replies.
Recommended three tiers based on both sets of evidence.

decisions.why: The 14 conversations showed which features office managers bundled in their heads, so the survey could name tiers in their own words.

decisions.choice: Price Growth at $29, inside the acceptable range of $21 to $36
decisions.why: The middle tier stayed in the band buyers called acceptable, and Starter gave small offices a cheaper way in.

hrtech-pricing.learned: Interviewing first meant the survey used the buyers' own words, and the price ranges came back tighter.

rules-latency.context: Pinewick quoted in the order tool, picked in the warehouse system and billed in the ledger, and each one rounded differently: by line, by order or at the total.
what_i_did: Collected 600 disputed invoices and traced each cent of difference to the step that rounded it.
Wrote one rule with Dennis Hale: round once, at the invoice total, after tax.
Specified one shared rounding function and had the quote tool, the pick list and the ledger export all call it.

decisions.choice: Round once at the invoice total, not on every line
decisions.why: Dennis's spreadsheet showed 71% of mismatches began with per-line rounding in the quote tool, which is where cents appeared and vanished.

decisions.choice: Publish the rule as one page with ten worked examples
decisions.why: Dennis would sign off numbers, not paragraphs, and sales could check a quote by hand.

rules-latency.learned: Splitting disputes by account size as well as in total showed the fix helped small accounts most, where a few cents is a phone call.

teardowns.context: Margin Notes is a one-page weekly newsletter. Every issue picks one product choice near me and asks about the change, the audience and the next experiment.
what_i_did: Issue 11, why the hardware store by the depot moved its returns desk to the front door: it turns returns from a hidden chore into a visible service.
Issue 26, the courier app that shows a 90-minute window instead of "tomorrow": a bet on calm over precision. My suggested test: the window alone against the window plus an exact time.
Each issue closes with a single test, so readers have something specific to argue with.
teardowns.problem: I wanted a weekly habit that forced me to defend one product opinion in print.

decisions.why: One change is small enough to explain, judge and test in a single sitting; a whole-business review is not.

decisions.choice: Close each issue with a test
decisions.why: It admits what I cannot know and hands readers a concrete thing to answer.

teardowns.learned: One decision and one test per issue is what kept a weekly rhythm alive next to the day job and the diploma.
